title: bps steady chair piles pressure new ceo 2026 09 02
author: Yawen Chen
text:
LONDON, Sept 2 (Reuters Breakingviews) - BP (BP.L)
, opens new tab
 is hoping to turn the page on a lengthy boardroom drama by selecting a steady pair of hands. Ian Tyler is the $115 billion oil major’s third permanent chair
, opens new tab
 in ​less than a year, following Helge Lund’s departure and Albert Manifold’s abrupt exit in May. Promoting the interim chair may soothe ‌investor jitters. But Tyler’s record as an operator offers less reassurance, leaving CEO Meg O’Neill to shoulder much of the execution burden alone.
Tyler brings obvious advantages. The former Balfour Beatty (BALF.L)
, opens new tab
 boss joined BP’s board in April 2025 and stepped in as interim chair after Manifold left. He has extensive boardroom experience, from defence group BAE ​Systems (BAES.L)
, opens new tab
 to miner Anglo American (AAL.L)
, opens new tab
. Former BAE Chair Roger Carr, who worked with Tyler for years, describes him as calm, measured and ​collegiate, able to push through change without creating "unnecessary turbulence". After BP’s latest bout of upheaval, that temperament has ⁠clear appeal.
The bigger question is how this calm demeanor squares with BP’s overhaul. Manifold’s short tenure added further momentum to the company’s current reset, ​pushing for faster disposals, tighter cost discipline and a more decisive tilt back towards fossil fuels. Tyler lowers the risk of another disruptive handover, but ​his record as boss of Balfour Beatty inspires less confidence.
During Tyler’s eight year tenure as chief executive, the UK building group delivered a total shareholder return of just 13%. The FTSE 100 Index (.FTSE)
, opens new tab
 returned 80% over the same period, while French rival Vinci (SGEF.PA)
, opens new tab
 delivered 96% and Sweden’s Skanska (SKAb.ST)
, opens new tab
 140%. The companies operated in different markets ​and had different business mixes, but Balfour’s underperformance is still stark.
This puts more weight on O’Neill’s shoulders. BP has already pivoted back to oil ​and gas, set tougher financial goals and is chasing billions of dollars of structural cost cuts while selling assets to simplify the portfolio and cut debt. ‌Investors will ⁠judge her less on strategy than on whether she can deliver more savings and execute further disposals.
BP can reasonably argue it is not looking for a second chief executive. Tyler’s job is to oversee the board and challenge management while O’Neill runs the business. After recent governance turmoil, a less interventionist chair may even be preferable.
Still, there is plenty of room between acting as a second CEO and being insufficiently challenging. Tyler looks ​well suited to restoring order but ​less obviously equipped to help O’Neill ⁠push through deeper change. Oil at around $95 a barrel should help cash flow and debt reduction, but it may make it harder to distinguish better execution from a favourable price backdrop.
Tyler may be exactly the chair ​BP needs. But calming the board is one thing; delivering better returns from BP’s reset will fall ​more squarely on ⁠O’Neill.
